title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to rank, classify, and prioritize documents in litigation and regulatory investigations. The scope includes early case assessment, relevance and privilege review, issue coding, and quality control of human decisions. It is used where document populations are too large for linear manual review, and it is typically governed by a discovery protocol agreed between parties or ordered by a court. sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review cover the use of machine learning to rank, classify, and prioritize documents in litigation and regulatory investigations. The scope includes early case assessment, relevance and privilege review, issue coding, and quality control of human decisions. It is used where document populations are too large for linear manual review, and it is typically governed by a discovery protocol agreed between parties or ordered by a court. The page describes current practice rather than advising a reader on any specific matter.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard e-discovery processing and review platforms that combine text extraction, search indexes, and a review database. Documents are typically converted to searchable text through optical character recognition and filtering, then loaded into a review workspace where coding decisions are recorded. The machine learning component operates inside or alongside that workspace, using the platform's existing search and metadata infrastructure rather than a separate training cluster. Most deployments are cloud-based or on-premises within the law firm or vendor environment, with no special hardware beyond ordinary server capacity.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A review team codes a seed set of documents for relevance or another issue, and the system learns from those examples to score the remaining population. In continuous active learning, the model repeatedly selects the documents most likely to change its understanding, presents them for human coding, and retrains until the gain in new relevant material falls below an agreed threshold. Validation uses a statistically sampled control set that is coded independently and withheld from training, allowing the team to estimate recall, precision, and richness. The process is iterative and documented, with decisions recorded for later audit.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are defensibility, inconsistent coding, and the possibility that a model misses a category of documents because the training examples were too narrow. Courts generally accept technology-assisted review where the parties agree on a protocol, the process is documented, and the results are tested against a control set. Privilege and confidentiality require that review decisions and model outputs remain within the protected discovery environment, and that any inadvertent production can be addressed through clawback arrangements. Provenance matters because every relevance call must be traceable to a human decision, a model prediction, or a quality-control step. This page describes practice and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Large language models are beginning to supplement traditional predictive coding by generating summaries, answering issue-specific questions, and making first-pass relevance calls on documents that a linear classifier would rank only by similarity. The next stage is likely to combine continuous active learning with generative review, where a model proposes a coding rationale and a human confirms or corrects it. Quality control is shifting from sampling entire populations to auditing model explanations and edge cases. As courts and parties gain more experience with these tools, protocols are likely to become more standardized, but the core requirement of a defensible, documented process will remain.
